title: oids: Manually recurse directories to create smiLib path
description:
The smiLib library itself does not recurse the path(s) set by smiSetPath().  Create functions to "manually" recurse the preference path(s) of "SMI Paths"

Now that Wireshark can recurse MIB directories, use the full directory structure provided by the latest libsmi share

Fixes #21089
Ping #15566

AI-Assisted: no

notes.body: @geraldcombs - Does Stratoshark even use smiLib?  Seems like a good time to just remove that functionality from the installer.
It theoretically could, if a syscall or log message included an OID. I think for now it would be better to just remove libsmi support.
Remove libsmi for just Stratoshark, right?  Otherwise this patch will look very different...

The recursing of the MIB directories could be a separate commit/MR, but I thought the two went hand in hand (and now we're not overwriting MIBs like is currently done trying to make a flat directory structure)

Especially since this directory is given by the user in a UAT, does this need some kind of check that either normalizes the path name or looks up the inode and skips descending into a subdirectory if it's already in the list? (Don't just use the raw name.) Otherwise infinite loops due to dumb hard or soft link tricks are possible.

Is the ws_dir_* API enough protection for the path name?
I did just add the check to prevent recursion on duplicate directory names.

I don't think it is. `wsutil/filesystem.h` has `files_identical`, which does the right thing on both POSIX and Windows for comparing two files, but we don't have a nice API for putting the results of those into a hash so we're not calling slow functions all the time, though that can be used as the basis of a hash table.
Created files_identical_hash to implement what I think your idea is.

The change you made it is good, but what I meant is that using `g_int_equal` doesn't (I am pretty sure) compare the hashes, it is operated on the items in the table themselves, which means it will cast the `char *` to a `int *` and compare them, which probably isn't what we want.
So is it okay to switch to g_str_equal and compare the "raw" string path at that point?

Not unless the strings have been normalized at that point, because otherwise they would compare differently, which means that the hash table would allow both to be inserted with keys that hashed to the same value (bucket collisions do happen with hashes.) Since we're not normalizing the path strings, we have to do the full comparison.

It's possible, theoretically, for two different files to have the same hash, because the hash is 32-bit but the inodes and the similar thing that Microsoft uses are larger. The hash table stores the 32-bit hashes and then only will call the (slower) equality comparison for files that hash the same.

You need to revert the changes to `files_identical`, and then instead of `g_int_equal` or `g_str_equal` pass in `files_identical` itself (or a small wrapper to give it the proper signature) as the equality function.

Applied the files_identical to the hash table, but should I consider a "local" function to handle it so we aren't using more gboolean "publicly"?  It's obviously the function signature of GHashTable, but it looks like for most of the Wireshark source base it's confined to static functions internal to a single source file.

Somewhat related - In testing the final "path string", it's clear that iterating through the hash table doesn't have the paths in "preference order" of that UAT.  Couldn't that matter if there are MIB files of the same name (and "first" should take precedence)?  Should I switch to more of a "list" (and "manually" have to check for uniqueness)?
Good suggestion!  Done.

The hash is good, but files can technically be different with the same hash.

What I would do is have everything up to computing `key` be a common static helper function, and then `files_identical` does a `memcmp` of two keys, whereas `files_identical_hash` hashes the key. We might want to use a common hash function, such as `wmem_strong_hash` too.
That looks done and I approve (and squashed the changes into the original commit)
